newsitem.title: USA: Utility competition opens door to technology firms.
newsitem.headline: Utility competition opens door to technology firms.

text.p: Technology companies see lucrative opportunities to provide new products and services to U.S. electric utilities seeking a competitive edge as the giant power industry moves into a deregulated marketplace.
Executives from several technology firms, here for the annual Edison Electric Institute Conference, expressed enthusiasm that utilities would need their expertise to survive deregulation.
"We're looking to change with our customers," said Jan van Dokkum, chief executive officer of Siemens Power Transmission and Distribution LLC, a U.S. subsidiary of Germany giant Siemens AG.
Industry analysts estimate the market for information technology products and services for the global utility industry at $10-15 billion, of which 40 percent is in the U.S.
They predict utilities will seek ways to "data-mine" loads of existing but under-used customer information to create customer profiles and tailor services and products to meet their particular needs.
"We are helping utilities by knowing who their customers are," said David Lieberman, industry sector manager at Siemens Business Communication Systems Inc, another U.S. Siemens AG affiliate.

Better knowledge of customer energy requirements and usage patterns, for example, would help utilities hang onto existing customers as regulators allow customers to shop for their own power provider, said Ulf Gundemark, a general manager at IBM's Utilities and Energy Services Industry division.
"It is cheaper to keep old customers and to be aware which customers are in the risk zone," Gundemark said.
"Customer retention is the one topic we talk about the most in the industry," said van Dokkum.
Executives also anticipate growing demand for utilities to find technological solutions to improve efficiencies with their operations to drive down costs.
For example, utilities could cut costs by automating tasks such as meter-reading and substation operation which are now being done manually, van Dokkum said.
Technology companies are forming joint ventures and new subsidiaries, and intensifying research efforts with the aim of becoming "one-stop shops" for utilities.
They are offering a range of products and services to utilities from short-term consulting to long-term outsourcing.
IBM opened a research center in Houston a year ago dedicated to developing new technologies for utilities.
Siemens Business Communication Systems announced Monday it has formed a joint venture with SABRE Decision Technologies to market real-time data technology for the U.S. utility sector.

"It's a patchwork right now in marketing...It will be an improved situation," said George Roberts, national sales manager in the U.S. for Schlumberger, one of the world's largest providers of electric meters.
